explanation: For each nonempty prefix, record the length of a dictionary word that can finish a decomposition. First test the whole prefix, then try reachable earlier word boundaries. Reconstruct backward using those lengths and reverse the words.
timeComplexity: O(n³) worst case including substring copying and hashing: O(n²) candidate cuts can each inspect O(n) characters. There are O(n²) candidate cuts; constructing and hashing candidate substrings costs up to O(n) per cut.
spaceComplexity: O(n) boundary lengths, transient substring characters and output characters. One predecessor or final-word length is stored per character boundary; output and transient substring characters are linear.

correctness: A recorded last length proves the earlier prefix is decomposable and the suffix is a dictionary word. Conversely every valid decomposition supplies such an earlier boundary. These implications prove reachability, and stepping backward by positive recorded lengths reconstructs a complete sequence.
walkthrough: For "sunleaf" and {"sun","leaf","sunl"}, prefix "sun" becomes reachable at 3 and "sunl" at 4. Only the split after 3 can finish with dictionary word "leaf", so reconstruct ["sun","leaf"]. JSON arguments are [domain,dictionary,canDecompose]. The last Boolean belongs only to the validator. The callable takes the first two arguments and returns words; observed true means that output satisfied the feasibility oracle.
edgeCases: Return an empty list when no decomposition exists.
A dictionary word may be used repeatedly.
Any valid word sequence is accepted; do not require a single predetermined split.
An empty input has the empty decomposition; the wrapper distinguishes feasibility using its separate Boolean oracle.
